newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian middle class growing, reluctant to invest.
newsitem.headline: Russian middle class growing, reluctant to invest.

text.p: A small but growing middle class is emerging in Russia, but its members are reluctant to provide the investment needed to kick the economy into growth, a senior government official said Monday.

"The important thing is not the rich or the poor, but what is between them," Yury Yurkov, the chairman of the State Statistics Committee, told a news conference. "The middle class is forming ..." he said.

Yurkov said investors, average Russians who could fuel growth by investing their savings, still hesitate to put their money in Russia. "Nineteen ninety-seven is not sure to bring an investment boom," he said.
Economic growth has eluded Russia since reforms began in earnest in 1992, but Yurkov said some indicators showed indirectly that Russians' lot is starting to improve.

Russians own about twice as many cars as in 1990, up to 15.2 million at the beginning of December from 8.7 million in 1990, extremely low for a population of nearly 150 million but a sharp rate of growth, he said.
Real incomes, which take into account inflation, were flat for the year, he said, and hidden income earned but not taxed made up 11 percent of gross domestic product.
Russian officials have often said the economy will spring into growth next year -- the same promise they made for 1996.
The 1997 budget, which faces final approval by parliament, forecasts 2 percent growth in GDP, the broadest indicator of output.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has repeatedly referred to 1997 as a "breakthrough year."

But overall figures indicate that the economy is still shrinking. GDP fell 6 percent over the year, a bigger loss than 1995's fall of 4 percent, while industrial output fell 5 percent after 3 percent in 1995.
"The problem with industrial growth is temporary," Yurkov said.
Analysts have said that presidential and parliamentary elections in the last 13 months and President Boris Yeltsin's November heart surgery undermined growth this year.
Foreigners were wary of investing in Russia, and domestic industry was more focused on politics than economics, some say.
Parliament's failure to adopt the 1997 budget, awaiting a final reading, further undermined investor confidence.

Yeltsin, who said he had recovered from surgery, returned to work on Monday, promising to put the country in order. "The doctors have done their job and now it is up to the president," he said in a television interview on Friday.
But Yurkov said average Russians have hesitated to invest their money in their own country -- foreign currency buying made up 22 percent of spending in November, against 13.5 percent in January.
He said some Russians were more interested in liquidity than profitable investments, despite slowing inflation, which fell to about 1 percent monthly in December from 3.2 percent a year ago.
"Our population, so far is not becoming an investor. It is giving credit to the American government," he said.
